Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00949

The answer, as we can learn from Avicenna’s books, is that the meaning of substance that serves as a broad category and names these natures is not simply “something that exists and does not exist in something else.” That meaning could not serve as a broad category. If it did, the feature that separates one kind within the category from another would have to make up the category itself. But a broad category does not need the features that divide it in order to be what it is. It needs them only for the category to exist in one definite way or another. Each such feature brings about an actual kind of the category; it does not combine with the category to form its basic meaning. So if the meaning of a category were actual existence together with the condition “not in something else,” then the feature that divides it into kinds would both bring about its existence and make up its meaning and nature, as we explained earlier.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00950

There is another reason. If 'substance' meant 'something that actually exists on its own,' then the nature of a kind would change whenever one of its individual members ceased to exist. The same view would also lead to more than one Necessary Being. A nature in itself is not brought into being or affected by a cause. If existence were identical with a nature, or part of it, then that nature would be eternally necessary. God, the one who sustains all, is far above having any partner or equal. Things that can either exist or not exist, by contrast, are nothing but their dependence on a cause; their very being is need for the one who brings them into being.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00951

Likewise, our phrase “something that actually exists” cannot be the basic meaning that defines substance. Otherwise, anyone who understood something that was a substance by nature would also know that it actually exists. The meaning of substance that can serve as a broad category is this: a thing with a nature that, if it existed outside the mind, would not exist in something else. This remains true whether its nature exists in thought or outside it. Its presence in the mind does not stop it from being the kind of thing that, if it existed outside the mind, would exist in itself. In this sense, the mental idea of substance is still substance.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00952

Another point confirms this. Calling something a substance in this sense does not depend on an outside cause. But saying that it actually exists—and that it exists in itself rather than in something else—does depend on an outside cause. That is not an essential feature, which belongs to a thing without needing another cause. If adding a negative condition, “not in something else,” made a highest category, then adding a positive condition, “in something else,” should make one too—and this case would be even stronger. But that is not the accepted view. This explains what they mean when they say that the mental idea of substance is substance.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00953

There is a further point to keep in mind. We will explain it when we discuss what it means to say that one thing is another. A concept can mean “what exists in itself” and yet be applied to something that exists in something else. Think of ideas such as nothingness, nonbeing, impossibility, a partner to God, a letter, a position, movement, and infinity. As ideas in the mind, they exist; by their meaning, they may point to what is absent, impossible, or dependent. The same idea can be called both, depending on which sense we mean.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00954

This explains why an idea of a substance can also be called a feature of the mind. What the idea represents is a substance; the idea itself depends on the mind in which it exists. There is no contradiction here. A contradiction would arise only if we placed one thing under two categories that are essential to different kinds of things.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00955

Some philosophers count forms of knowledge as qualities. This seems to mean that a mental idea of a substance is both substance and quality, and so belongs to two categories. They explain the word “quality” in one of two ways. If it means a kind of thing whose existence outside the mind depends on something else, and which does not itself involve size or relation, then it is a separate basic category, opposed to substance. In that sense, one thing cannot belong to both categories. But if “quality” means more broadly a feature that, when it actually exists, does not of itself involve size or relation, then it is a general term that can apply to all the basic kinds when they exist in the mind. In that broader sense, it does not conflict with substance or with the other kinds normally called qualities. This is how their argument should be understood. We will give our own account later.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00956

Be clear about this: when philosophers say that the universals of substances are substances, they do not mean that a mental idea of substance, though it is in the mind, is independent of the mind. Nor do they mean that this same mental form can leave the mind and return, existing at one time outside the mind without a subject and at another time in the mind as something that depends on it. That would be like a magnet in the hand: outside the hand it attracts iron, but when held in the hand it does not. That comparison fails if we forget the difference between a general idea and a particular thing, or between what a thing is and how it exists. The universal idea, as something in the mind, cannot move outside the mind or become independent of a subject. A particular magnet can move from one place to another and remain the same individual magnet, attracting iron in one place but not in another. Mental forms are not like that.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00957

By “universal substance,” they mean the nature of a thing considered by itself, without adding that it is general, particular, or joined to any other condition from thought or the outside world. This is sometimes called the natural universal. It differs from a nature already considered as universal, which is called the intellectual universal. The intellectual universal cannot exist as a particular thing outside the mind, but the nature considered by itself can. Because it is so open-ended, that nature can be joined to many conditions that do not fit together, such as being one or many, existing in something else or in itself, and being an object of thought or of sense. So although the mental idea of substance is a quality because of its particular existence in the mind and its generality, it is substance by its nature: if that nature existed outside the mind, it would not exist in something else.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00958

When philosophers compare an intelligible substance to a magnet, they mean only this: the magnet’s nature includes the ability to attract iron, whatever its current state. If it is held in a person’s hand and does not attract iron, or is placed beside iron and does attract it, we do not say that it has changed its nature. In both cases it is the same kind of stone, with the ability to attract iron. This much is enough to make the comparison useful.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00959

Someone may object that Avicenna says in The Healing and elsewhere that the features which distinguish kinds of substances do not themselves have to be substances by nature. Although the word “substance” can be applied to them, it applies as an incidental feature, not as part of what they are. This avoids an endless chain in which every distinguishing feature would need another feature to distinguish it. But if these features are not part of the category of substance, they must belong to another category of qualities. Then one and the same thing would be both substance and quality in the same existence, since each kind and its distinguishing feature are one.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00960

Even if the feature that distinguishes one kind of substance from another is not itself a substance, it does not follow that it belongs to some other basic class or must be a quality. Neither reason nor religious teaching rules out simple natures with no broader kind or distinguishing feature from any of the categories. Avicenna states this in the section on categories in The Healing.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00961

A theologian offered an answer to this problem: how can the same thing be a substance and a quality, general and particular, knowledge and the thing known? When we think of something, he says, two things arise. First comes a general idea, which the mind knows. It is present in the mind as a thing can be present in time or space, but it is not a feature of the mind. Second comes the individual act of knowing, a quality that belongs to the mind. On this view, there is no problem. The problem arises only if the same thing is both substance and quality, or both knowledge and known, or both general and particular.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00962

If these are two ways of considering one thing, as the philosophers and careful thinkers hold, his answer may explain how something can be both knowledge and what is known, or both general and particular. But it still does not explain how the same thing can be both a substance and a quality. If, instead, he means that they are two different things, then his view goes against experience and reason, and introduces a third position without proof. It also leads to this: every immaterial form that exists on its own is aware of itself and known to itself. Philosophers use this to explain how God knows Himself and how spiritual beings know themselves. So, by his account, whenever the human soul thinks of something, it creates or brings into being an immaterial intellect that knows and acts by itself. He has admitted that an intelligible thing arises when we think of something, and that this thing is not in the mind or in anything else.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00963

But the soul cannot bring an independently existing intellect into being, not even by preparing for its arrival. The soul can receive things it understands, but that ability is only a potential one. Something already able to act must bring it into use. If the soul produces such an intellect, it must either be the source that gives it existence or merely prepare a place to receive it. The first is impossible: what exists only as a possibility cannot make something actual in itself. The second does not fit his view, because whatever is prepared to receive something must be its subject. If the soul is neither its source nor the subject that receives it—and is not its goal or form either—then there is no connection by which it could bring the intellect into being. Moreover, something that comes into being or changes cannot itself be an intellect fully actual in itself, as their own principles make clear.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00964

His view also makes the known thing general and particular at the same time. It is general because it is understood apart from the features that distinguish particular things. But if it exists on its own rather than depending on the mind, it must itself be particular, since anything that exists outside the mind is particular. Here is the point. Individual things of the same kind differ in their outward features. If we grasp what they have in common without those features, that shared nature must be present to us in a different way. It cannot be called general or shared among many unless it exists for something that strips away the features that prevent it from applying to many. A thing’s being stripped of those features cannot be separated from its existence for the thing that strips them away. And this stripped existence must be the very existence the nature has for that mind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00965

If a nature’s existence in a stripped form is the same as its existence for the mind—the mind that draws ideas from particular material things and removes their material features—then the nature must exist for the mind as something that depends on it. That is the only way it can be present there. For something to exist in a subject means that its existence in itself is the very same as its existence for that subject. From this we can see the position taken by those who accept mental existence. In brief, particular forms of sense and imagination depend on the soul as an action depends on its source. They are images that the soul brings about in the lesser imagination, the imagination joined to the soul, not in a greater imagination that exists apart from it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00966

General forms are different. On this account, they are intellectual beings that exist apart from the soul, but the soul can reach them. Because it sees them indistinctly, it takes a single form to be something that could apply to many things. This is like a person with weak eyesight who sees a dim shape and cannot tell whether it is Zayd, Amr, or someone else. Since these intellects exist more fully than the soul, they cannot be effects produced by the soul or forms that exist within it as its own products. The soul is a place where they appear. This is the position he takes. It rests on the view that mental forms are immaterial, that the soul has an imagination joined to it, and that there are universal intellectual forms. He accepts all three.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00967

We can raise two objections to this view. The first is that being a cause or an effect, being material or immaterial, and similar features belong only to real existence outside the mind. Mental existence, which has none of the effects that belong to real things, cannot have these features. The author himself says in his discussion of creation that bringing something into being is a feature of external existence. He also lists mental existence at the beginning of this inquiry as distinct from both immaterial and material existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00968

Here is the second objection. He says that an idea has a weaker existence than a thing outside the mind. Yet he also says that images and beings known through the intellect exist more fully than material things. This seems to make the mental images of particular and universal things both stronger and weaker than the things they represent. The image of Zayd represents the actual Zayd; the idea of a human being applies to actual human beings. Since these images belong to the imaginal and intellectual worlds, they should be stronger than their examples. Yet because they exist in the mind, they should be weaker. So they would be both stronger and weaker than what they represent. That is a contradiction.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00969
Both objections confuse questions that need to be kept apart. Once we distinguish them and explain what it means for something to exist in the mind, the difficulty disappears.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00970

The proofs for mental existence establish that the very things which exist outside also exist in another way: in that other mode, they do not produce the same effects they produce outside. By “effects” we mean everything true of a thing in the outside world, both what it is and the features it has. For example, Zayd as an object of thought is not a substance, a body, a living thing, an animal, or a human being. Nor does he have any of the further perfections of the actual Zayd. This is another mode of existence, different from external existence, where Zayd has both his basic features and his further perfections.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00971

This answers all the objections that expect a thing’s features in the outside world to appear in its mental existence as well. The proofs show that those external features are absent from mental existence. But this does not stop mental existence from having other features shared by existence in general, such as causing and being caused, being particular and distinct, or being free from matter. A feature that comes from a thing’s relation to something else is different from a feature that belongs to the thing in itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00972

We must therefore look at an idea in two ways. First, consider it as a picture of something outside the mind. The idea does not have the effects that the real thing has. This is what makes it a representation: it points beyond itself, and its role is to show what it represents. This is what we are discussing when we speak of mental existence. Second, consider the mental form in itself, apart from its relation to the external thing. It is something real, not nothing, and it can have features of its own. From this point of view, it may even have a fuller existence than the thing it represents. In this sense it is a real existence, not a mental one.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00973

This second aspect raises two further questions. First: when the mental form exists for us as an object, is it a quality of the mind, as most of the philosophers in Aristotle’s school say? Or is it a form that completes us: an imaginal or intellectual form with which the soul becomes one in knowing it, as matter takes on the form that shapes it? It will become clear later that a form and the feature that distinguishes it do not belong to one of the basic categories in themselves, but only incidentally. This seems to be Alexander of Aphrodisias’s view. Or is it a substantial form for our soul when we know substances, and a quality or further perfection when we know things that are themselves qualities? This is the question discussed in the theory of knowledge.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00974

The second question is this: what is the thing known by this act of knowing—the external thing that becomes clear to us? Is it a material example, with the soul removing some of its material features, as it does when we perceive particular things, or all of them, as it does when we grasp general ideas? That is the usual view. Or is the thing known a complete imaginal or intellectual being that exists in its own right and is free from matter?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00975

If it is such a being, then the soul, through the senses, connects in some way with the material world and becomes ready to see that imaginal or intellectual being in its own world. The soul then becomes one with it as knower and known, and receives a form from it. In this direct kind of knowing, the soul encounters the very thing it knows, existing outside it. Its connection with a material object then leads it to apply the form to that object and identify the object as what the form represents. The form does not produce the effects of the material thing. This gives us a second kind of knowing: knowing something through an idea of it. These are the questions to keep in mind so that the arguments in each discussion remain clear.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00976

Several points follow from this. First, the effects absent from mental existence include both a thing’s basic features and its further perfections. Second, mental existence is relative: it is what a thing is for a knower, and it ends when that relation ends. This is what it means for the mental form to represent something beyond itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00977

Third, whenever we know something through an idea, that knowledge is also accompanied by direct awareness. If the form in its physical example had no connection to or presence in the soul, it would be particular and perceptible, not general and intelligible. It would not yet have been freed from the material coverings that keep it from being an object of thought. Yet we have assumed that it is intelligible to the soul and exists there in a way different from its material existence, which comes with those coverings. Think about this. Now suppose both the known thing and the soul exist in their own right, free from matter. In what sense could one be inside the other? And why should the soul contain the thing rather than the other way around?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00978

One independently existing thing can literally contain another only when both have size, as bodies do. Still, someone whose heart has been lit by God and who has tasted some of the knowledge of spiritual beings may accept what we suggested at the start: in relation to what we sense and imagine, the soul is more like an active maker than a passive container. This answers many objections to mental existence that assume the soul is a place where perceptions sit, and that for something to exist in another thing means it is inside it. These objections include saying that the soul is the matter of substantial forms, that a substance becomes a quality, and that the soul takes on features it does not have, such as heat, cold, movement, rest, being even or odd, or the nature of a horse or a stone.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00979

If perceptions arise through the soul without being lodged inside it, these problems fall away. Nor do we need to split what the soul perceives from what becomes present to it. This is clear for things perceived by the outer senses and by the inner senses.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00980

The soul relates to universal intellectual forms through an illuminating connection to intellectual realities in the creative world. Their relation to bodily kinds is like the relation, in the familiar account, between ideas drawn from individual material things and those things themselves. Although these intellectual realities exist in their own right and are individuals, the soul’s perception of them is weak in this world because it is tied to dense bodily things. It can see them only partly, like something far away in dusty air, or like a person with weak eyesight who sees a shape from a distance and cannot tell whether it is Zayd, Amr, Bakr, or Khalid—or whether it is a person, a tree, or a stone. In the same way, an illuminated form or intellectual reality may seem unclear to the soul.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00981

Generality, vagueness, and the ability of one idea to apply to many are signs of weak existence or weak understanding. This weakness may come from the knower: the power to understand may be weak, like a child’s, or something may prevent it from working fully, as happens to souls tied to the body in this dark world. But the weakness may also come from what is known. This can happen because it is faint or incomplete, like time, number, and basic matter.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00982

Or the thing known may be too great and bright for the soul to grasp fully, as with the higher beings known through the intellect. Their beauty and brightness may overwhelm our understanding. This is why the mind cannot fully grasp the Necessary Being, God.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00983

In short, when the soul understands general ideas, it sees immaterial intellectual beings. It does not do this by stripping an idea from something sensed, as most philosophers say. Rather, it travels from what it senses to what it imagines, then to what it understands; from this world to the next and beyond; from the world of bodies to the world of imaginal forms, then to the world of intellects. The Qur'anic verse “You know the first creation. Why, then, do you not reflect?” points to this. We truly understand the next life by knowing this one, because two things that are related can be understood through one another.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00984

We have almost left the subject at hand, so let us return. Knowledge, then, is a kind of existence, a form of existence that belongs to the perceiving soul or is present to it, as we will explain later. Every substantial or accidental existence is accompanied by a general nature, which the people of spiritual insight call the “fixed essence.” We hold that in itself it is neither existent nor nonexistent.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00985

Nor does this fixed essence have any of the features of existence, such as being a cause or an effect, coming before or after something, and the like. As we have explained, what exists in itself, whether it is sensed or understood, has either material or immaterial existence. Its nature is joined to it and exists through it. In the same way, what is present to our powers of perception—the thing known, witnessed, or held before them—exists as a sensory or intellectual form.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00986

Sensory forms begin to exist independently of the human soul and appear before it in another world through something that reveals them, such as the eye, a mirror, or the imagination, without being inside those things. Intellectual forms, by contrast, are reached when the soul rises toward them and connects with them; they do not enter the soul. These intellects are particular in themselves, but their natures can apply to many individuals of their kinds.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00987

In each of these ways of existing, the thing’s nature appears along with it, but only as a dependent image. Think of a clear reflection in a polished mirror. The reflection is a likeness; it is not itself the kind of independent thing, or the quality, that it shows. The image of a person seen in a mirror is not an actual human being; it exists only because the person exists. In the same way, the ideas of animal, plant, movement, and heat that appear in the mind are the meanings of those things, not the things themselves. A concept does not have to be an example of the thing it means.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00988

In short, when external things come before the human soul, the soul’s freedom from matter allows sensory, imaginal, and intellectual forms to appear in it, as reflections appear in a mirror. The difference is that the mirror receives its image, while the soul brings its forms about through its own activity.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00989

Do not take this to be the same as the view that mental forms are only copies or likenesses. That view says that a person’s essence exists in the outside world, while only its shadow or copy—not its essence—is present in the mind. We hold instead that human nature, or its fixed essence, is preserved in both places, though it does not exist by itself in either. Rather, it is joined to different kinds of existence in different ways.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00990

For example, outside the mind, the idea of a human being is joined to an existence that can be described as a substance with dimensions, growth, sensation, and the ability to understand intellectual realities. In another kind of existence, it is a separate intellectual substance, which Plato and earlier philosophers called the Holy Spirit. In the mind, it is joined to yet another kind of existence: a mental quality that cannot be divided or related, and that exists either as a passing state or as a settled ability.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00991

When we say that something is something else, we can mean two different things. In the first sense, we say that an actual thing has a particular description. The thing we are talking about is one example of what that description covers. The claim may be about the subject as a concept or about the particular things it applies to. What is said may describe what the thing is or add a feature to it. All these are ordinary predication, whether the claim is essential or incidental.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00992

The second kind means that the subject is precisely the meaning and nature of the predicate, though we still notice a difference between them. The predicate names the subject’s nature; it does more than say that the two share an existence. This is the first, or essential, way of saying something about a thing. It tells us what the thing is by its very nature, not merely a feature it happens to have. That is why it comes first when we affirm or deny something about the thing. A single claim can be both true and false of the same subject, depending on which kind of predication we mean. The same concept can even be said of itself in one sense and denied of itself in another. For example, something is particular by its definition, but the idea of “particular” is general in ordinary predication because it applies to many things. The concept of a grammatical particle is a particle by definition, but as a word it is a noun.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00993

With this distinction in place, we can say that general natures known by the intellect do not belong to any basic category insofar as they are general ideas. But insofar as they exist in the soul as a state or ability—and the soul either shows them or brings them about—they fall under the category of quality as features of the soul.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00994

You may ask: if something is a substance, does that not form part of its very nature? And are size and relationships not part of the natures of things that have them? My friend, there is an important difference. Calling a human being a substance when we define what a human being is does not turn the definition itself into a substance. The concept of “particular,” for example, is itself not particular, even though its meaning is what cannot apply to many things. A thing’s definition may express its nature, but that does not make the definition an example of the thing.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00995

Likewise, saying that the concept of substance is identical with itself does not make it one of the substances or kinds of substance. The same applies to the other categories. It would follow only if the effects of the category applied to the concept. For example, if the idea of substance, considered as a general idea, existed outside the mind, it would have to exist independently of a subject. But a general idea cannot exist outside the mind, because every actual thing outside the mind is particular. The same holds for most definitions. The definition of animal—“a living, sensing substance”—does not itself fit that definition by ordinary predication, though it does by primary predication.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00996

Someone might object: if the natures of kinds do not themselves belong to the categories, in any mode of existence, then the categories are not essential to those natures or true of them in any sense. Nor would actual individuals belong to those categories, since a thing’s reality is its kind. We reply that belonging to a category requires two things. First, the concept of that category must be part of what the thing is. For example, a surface is a continuous quantity that is stable and divisible in two directions. These ideas form parts of its definition. Second, the effects of the category must apply to it: because it is a quantity, it can be divided and compared; because it is continuous, its parts can meet along shared boundaries; and because it is stable, its parts exist together.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00997

Now consider what happens when things of a given kind exist outside the mind. Their defining features have real effects, because the things themselves exist. But when we think about that kind, the idea still contains the meaning of those features without producing their effects. Effects belong to things, not to the ideas we have of them.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00998

For example, the idea of a surface contains the meaning of quantity. But the idea itself does not divide into parts. As something that exists in the mind and depends on it, it is a simple, immaterial meaning. If that meaning existed outside the mind, the effects of quantity would follow from it. The same is true of the idea of a human being: it contains the general meaning “a living, rational being,” but it is not itself an animal with actual size, location, growth, sensation, or voluntary movement. It contains the meaning of animal and the meaning of reason, but not their actions and effects. The same is true of the idea of reason.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00999

Someone may object: you have separated a thing’s nature from effects that are actually part of its nature. To be a quantity is to be divisible. How, then, can the idea of a surface involve quantity but not itself be divisible? If it is divisible by its nature, it cannot be a quality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01000

We reply that the idea contains the meaning of quantity. The proofs for mental existence show only that the natures of things are present in the mind, not their individual examples or their particular modes of existence. We have already shown that modes of existence and individual features cannot move from one realm to another. The definition of knowledge as a form that comes from the thing known is enough to show this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01001

Applying the meaning of quantity to these kinds is like including the meaning of quantity in its own definition: the meaning is part of what they are. Just as the idea of quantity does not become an example of itself or divide into parts simply because it means “divisible,” neither do the kinds that appear in the mind become divisible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01002

What we have explained shows that mental ideas, considered as natures, are not examples of the basic categories. The category meanings are either the ideas themselves or part of them. But insofar as the ideas exist as features of the mind, they belong to the category of quality only incidentally, not by their nature. The original problem depends on assuming that every category is essential to each of its examples in every respect. No proof establishes this, and experience does not support it. This assumption has confused people: some deny mental existence, some say a thing’s nature changes, and some say that knowledge is called a quality only by a figure of speech. Each has chosen a different view, but none has found a satisfactory answer.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01003

The second objection is this: when we imagine high mountains, wide deserts with their trees and rivers, hills and valleys, or huge planets and stars, we imagine them as particular things. So, on their view, all of these must exist inside the power of imagination. Yet that power is not a body and has no size; it is a mental quality or power that depends on a small amount of vapor in the brain. When we imagine Zayd together with other people, does this tiny power contain people who perceive, move, understand, and carry on their trades and crafts? The mind is sure this is impossible. The same difficulty arises if the place of these images is said to be the spirit in the front of the brain: that too is small. A huge image cannot be imprinted in something tiny. It does not help to say that both can be divided without end. A hand cannot hold a mountain, even if both can be divided endlessly.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01004

This objection applies only to those who say that bodily likenesses and images exist inside the powers of imagination or sense. They have not proved this with a clear and sufficient argument, as anyone who follows their claims can see. These powers may prepare the soul to see images in a greater world of images that exists apart from it. That was Suhrawardi’s view, following the ancient Persian philosophers and the Stoics. Or they may be the means by which the soul makes images in its own smaller world, as I hold. In short, the objection does not apply to someone who says that sensed things have another kind of existence besides their bodily existence in the material world.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01005

The proofs for the existence of forms known by the soul show that there is another world, and that these images and likenesses exist in another way besides the way they appear to the outer senses. Through this other existence they appear to our inner powers. The soul, freed from both these kinds of existence and higher than both worlds, may even see them with the help of its inner powers, just as it sees images with the help of the outer senses.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01006

From what the outer senses perceive, the soul knows of the material world. From what its inner powers perceive, it knows of another world of images. And from its knowledge of itself and of realities grasped by the intellect, it knows of a third world beyond both. We remember particular people we once saw, even after they have disappeared from this world, and picture them with the same size, shape, and position. The image stands before us in its particular form. It must exist somewhere, though not in this material world, so it exists in another world.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01007

Plato, the ancient sages, and the mystics who saw these realities taught that the beings of the imaginal world exist without a place or direction. This world lies between the world of intellect and the world of sense. Intellectual beings are entirely free from matter and from place, shape, size, color, and light. Sensible beings are immersed in these features. Images in this middle world are different from both: they do not occupy a physical place, yet they still have size and shape.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01008

Here is the substance of Suhrawardi’s argument in The Wisdom of Illumination. Vision does not happen because the image of the thing seen is stamped on the eye, as Aristotle held, or because a ray leaves the eye and reaches the thing, as mathematicians said. Vision happens when a luminous object faces a healthy eye. This gives the soul direct awareness of the object, and so it sees it. The image in a mirror is not in the eye, since something large cannot be stamped into something small. Nor is the mirror image exactly the same as the person or thing seen, as some have thought.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01009

The image is not in the mirror or in any other body. The eye’s clear lens relates to visible things as a mirror relates to the images that appear in it. Since the mirror’s image is not in the mirror, the image perceived through the lens is not in the lens either. It appears when the soul’s direct awareness meets a luminous object and no obstacle blocks it. If the thing has an existence outside the mind, the soul sees it. If it is only an image, it needs something to show it, like a mirror.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01010

When the eye’s lens faces a mirror in which images appear, the soul’s direct awareness reaches those images through the lens and the mirror, when the right conditions are present and obstacles are removed. Just as the large image cannot be stamped into the eye, it cannot be stamped into a place in the brain. So imagined images are not in the mind, where a large thing could not fit into a small place. They are not in the outside world either, or everyone with healthy senses would see them. Nor are they nothing, since we can imagine and distinguish them and make different true or false claims about them. They exist in another region: the imaginal world, also called the separate imagination because it is not material like the imagination joined to the soul.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01011

This is the world whose existence was taught by ancient philosophers such as Plato, Socrates, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and other spiritual thinkers, as well as mystics from many peoples. They spoke of two worlds: the world of intellect, which includes the divine world and the worlds of intellects and souls; and the world of images, which includes sensory forms and imaginal images.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01012

Imaginal images are not Plato’s Forms. The greatest philosophers who believed in these images also believed in Plato’s Forms: great, fixed lights in the world of intellectual light. Imaginal images, by contrast, are suspended in the imaginal world. Some are dark, like the Hell that holds the suffering of the wretched; others are bright, like the gardens where the fortunate enjoy themselves. Those who are nearest to God rise to the highest level and dwell in the gardens of holiness among divine lights and sacred Forms.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01013

Here is an insight from beyond the Throne. I believe in a world of forms and dimensions that is not material, as the greatest philosophers and mystics taught and as Suhrawardi explained so fully. But I differ from him in two respects. First, I say that imagined images exist in a realm of the soul as soon as the soul forms them by its own power, using the imagination. They do not exist in a world outside the soul, created by some other power, as Suhrawardi’s words seem to imply. The imagination’s random play and the ugly images it makes—unlike the work of a wise creator—belong to the small inner world. They come from the imagination’s mischief.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01014

These images last as long as the soul attends to them and uses the imagination to form and hold them. When the soul turns away, they disappear. They do not continue to exist on their own, kept in place without the soul’s attention, as Suhrawardi thought. There is a difference between mere inattention and forgetting: when we are inattentive, the soul can still bring an image back without new sense experience. When we have forgotten it, we need a new experience or something that serves the same purpose, such as a reminder.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01015

The second point of difference is this: Suhrawardi says that images seen in mirrors exist in the imaginal world. We say they are shadows of things we sense. They have a shadow-like existence here: they are reflections that depend on real things, not things that exist in their own right. The same is true when someone sees double, or when a sound produces an echo. Neither the second image nor the echo exists on its own. Each depends on something outside it. As we have explained, everything apart from the modes of existence themselves depends on them, like a shadow or reflection depends on what it represents. A reflection is not the thing it reflects, as one mystic writes: “The whole world is the echo of His song—who has ever heard an echo so long?”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01016

A third objection is this: if things exist in the mind as you have argued, then every bodily kind and every kind of bodily quality must have an individual example that is free of matter and of its features, such as size, place, and position. That example would itself be both an individual and a general kind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01017

The objection runs as follows. On your account, every general idea we understand exists in the mind. Either it remains wholly unspecified there, without becoming an individual thing, or it becomes a particular thing. The first cannot be right, because existence always makes something particular. The idea of something existing while remaining wholly undefined makes no sense. The second means that when we understand “human being,” a particular human being—stripped of size, shape, and every other material feature—must appear in the mind. If those features remained with it, it could not exist in the immaterial intellect, according to the principles you accept. But this conclusion is plainly false, and everyone agrees it is. So the starting claim must be false as well.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01018

The usual reply is that what exists in the mind is a particular quality or state of the mind. It is not an example of the substance that the idea describes, though it is the very same meaning as that substance. The same answer applies to our ideas of bodily qualities. You already know from our answer to the first objection that what the mind receives from an external substance is its meaning, not the substance itself or one of its individual examples. The mental idea is general because we consider it apart from the features that make it particular, both in the mind and outside it. There is no contradiction in something being general in one respect and particular in another, especially when we compare its mental and external existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01019

If someone still insists that the idea of human nature in the mind shares the reality of actual human beings and is itself a substance, while existing in the mind as a state that the mind does not need, then that person has fallen into the same difficulty we have already described.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01020

It is strange that Mulla Dawwani insists that the mental meanings of substances are themselves substances. He says that a substance is a nature that can exist outside the mind without being in a subject. He criticizes anyone who says that the mental form of a substance is a quality, on the grounds that this would turn a substance into a quality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01021

Yet the change of a substance into a quality that he fears follows more directly from his own account, as careful thought will show. He can avoid this only by adding a condition to every definition of a substantial kind: “when it exists outside the mind.” If so, not only would the human being in the mind be a substance in this special sense; its ability to have dimensions, its size, growth, sensation, reason, and every feature contained in these ideas would also have to be qualified in the same way. Then there would be no real difference between saying that the mental form is truly a quality and saying, through these forced qualifications, that it is a kind of substance.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01022

In fact, the idea of a human being, like the ideas of other kinds of independently existing things, is a feature of the mind. It is human in what it means, but it is not itself an actual human being. That is the distinction between the two ways of saying what a thing is. For people who do not accept a separate intellectual world containing forms of substantial kinds—as Aristotle and his followers did—proofs of mental existence show no more than this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01023

But someone who believes in that higher intellectual world can say that some individual examples of a kind exist without matter, while others exist in matter. There is no clear proof or common-sense reason that this is impossible. Plato and the great philosophers before him held that every bodily kind has an individual in the world of intellect. These individuals are active causes of the bodily examples of their kinds, and care for them. The argument that individuals of one kind cannot differ in how complete or perfect they are applies, if it is sound at all, only when they share the same mode of existence and the same realm. It need not apply to individuals that exist in two different modes and realms.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01024

In truth, Plato’s view, and the view of the great philosophers before him, that there are intellectual Forms of bodily kinds is strong and well founded. Later thinkers’ objections do not stand. They arise because those thinkers did not reach the level of the earlier philosophers or understand what they meant, as we will explain later, God willing. Their conclusions rested on clear spiritual insights and sacred visions, not merely on arguments that invite doubt. One group after another has rejected the group before it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01025

Those great philosophers and saints did not set out a formal proof for these higher Forms. Instead, they reported clear visions they had experienced repeatedly. A person can trust what they all reported and accept that they were sure of what they saw. No one should debate them about this. If people accept the positions of the stars and the number of the heavenly spheres on the basis of observations made by Hipparchus, or a few people like him, using senses that often mislead, then it is even more fitting to accept the repeated intellectual observations of the leading philosophers, which cannot be mistaken.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01026

A fourth objection is this: if mental existence is real, then the mind must become hot when it thinks of heat, cold when it thinks of cold, curved or straight, round, triangular, or square, a disbeliever or a believer, and even something with a location. A hot thing is something in which heat exists, a cold thing something in which cold exists, and the same applies to other descriptions. So the soul would take on the features of bodies and even opposite features. This is plainly false.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01027

Here is the reasoning behind the objection. If the things we think about actually entered our minds, they would exist there as features of the mind. The mind would then have the very qualities it was thinking about.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01028

There are several replies. The first is an insight from beyond the Throne. When the soul imagines these things, their images appear in a realm of the soul; they do not take up residence inside the soul. Just as the soul, a radiant, immaterial being, shines through the power of sight and directly sees what faces the eye without an image being stamped into it—as the ancient philosophers held—so it shines through the imagination and directly sees an imagined image that exists outside the soul. The image is distinct from the soul; it does not enter the soul or make the soul take on its features.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01029

Just as the soul sees and senses external images through sight and the other outer senses, it sees inner images through its inner senses. These images do not live inside the soul itself. Our experience makes no distinction between seeing while awake and seeing by day.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01030

Second, even if imagined images exist in the soul as forms that enter it, the soul takes on a feature only when it is affected by that feature, not merely because the feature exists in it. The active sources that bring events in the world into being contain knowledge of the forms of those things, yet they do not take on the bodies’ qualities. The forms are present in those higher sources through their activity and their power to bring things about, not because those sources receive or suffer the effects of the forms. We do not accept that merely existing in something makes it take on the thing’s features unless it is affected or changed by it. Whether a word such as “hot” can be applied merely because heat is present is a separate question and does not concern us here.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01031

The second answer uses the distinction between two ways of saying that something is something else. The idea of disbelief is not itself an act or state of disbelief. Thinking about disbelief therefore does not make a person a disbeliever. The same is true of the other examples. Anyone seeking a way out of this objection should apply that distinction carefully.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01032

A third answer, given in the standard books, is that the objection confuses real existence with the lesser, image-like existence of an idea. A body is hot because actual heat exists in it, not because the mind has an idea of heat. Heat and cold are opposites as real things, not as ideas. The same applies to the other examples. Each of these qualities means that, when it exists in a material body, it puts the body in a certain state and has effects that the senses can detect. Heat, for example, separates unlike parts of a mixture and brings like parts together. A straight line is one whose parts lie along the same direction. The same is true of curves and other shapes. If we understand these ideas and they exist as states in the immaterial soul, this means only that the soul has ideas of things that can make bodies hot, cold, straight, curved, or otherwise shaped. It does not mean that the soul itself becomes a material thing with those features.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01033

Someone may reply that this answer fails for features that necessarily follow from what a thing is, or that we understand through a relationship. Consider evenness and oddness, necessity, causes, and parenthood. These are not external things. Nor does the answer work for features of things that do not exist, such as impossibility and nonexistence. We cannot say that the mind takes on these features only when they exist outside it, because they have no such existence. They are either ideas formed by the intellect or features of things that do not exist.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01034

We can answer this by applying what we have already established in this book: every meaning has some share of existence. Evenness, for example, exists in the sense that the thing it describes can be understood as divisible into two equal parts. That is its real mode of existence. But when the soul thinks of evenness, it does not itself become divisible into two equal parts. The same applies to other ideas. As for nonexistence and similar ideas, they have no image in the mind. The intellect actively turns some concepts into names or labels for things that cannot exist, and uses them to understand those things’ features.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01035

A fifth objection is this: the mind exists in the world, and the things we think about exist in the mind. So those things seem to exist inside something that itself exists in the world. Anything that exists inside one thing must also exist inside whatever contains that thing—like water in a jug that is in a house.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01036

We reply that something inside one thing is inside another only when both exist in their own right and are distinct things, like water in a jug and the jug in a house. What we know in the mind is different. It is present there as an image, not as a separate thing with its own independent existence. The mind, by contrast, has its own real existence in the outside world. So the word “in” has a different meaning in these two cases. The word is also used differently for being in a place or time. To exist in the outside world means to produce the effects proper to a thing; to exist in the mind means not to produce those same effects.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01037

A sixth objection is this: the theory seems to put real examples of impossible things inside our minds, not merely ideas of them. When we judge that contradictions cannot exist together, for example, we first imagine them. That imagined contradiction then exists in the mind as a particular thing. But common sense says that contradictions cannot exist in the mind or outside it. The same problem seems to arise for absolute nonexistence and for a partner to God: if an individual example of a partner to God exists in the mind, then, by its own nature, it must also exist outside the mind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01038

The answer is that when we speak of things that cannot exist, our statements are not unconditional. We are saying what would follow if the idea we have named could apply to an actual example. The intellect can form ideas of contradiction, a partner to God, an indivisible substance, and every other concept—including the idea of its own nonexistence, the nonexistence of its cause, nonexistence itself, and the idea of what cannot exist. It does not form these ideas as the realities of impossible things. Anything the mind forms as an idea is possible as an idea. Rather, the idea serves as a name for an impossible nature that cannot itself be pictured.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01039

For a concept to serve as a name for a nature, its meaning must fit that nature by essential predication, even if it does not fit by ordinary predication. The intellect can form an idea and, by supposition, use it as a name for a nature that cannot exist and cannot itself be pictured. Because the idea exists in the mind and points to an impossible nature, we can correctly say that it is impossible to judge or know that nature. We can speak about that impossibility even though we cannot speak about the nature itself. The claim can be made about the idea, which can exist in the mind. It cannot be made in the same way about the impossible thing that the idea names.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01040

The same kind of statement is made about the Necessary Being: for example, that its individuality is identical with its essence, or that its oneness differs from what we mean by “oneness.” The statement concerns the idea of the Necessary Being. But the claim that its individuality is identical with its essence concerns the reality that proof leads us to: God, the Living and Self-Subsisting, who is beyond being pictured in any mind. We can therefore see that these statements, and statements like them, are not plain, unconditional statements. Although they can be restated as conditionals, they do not simply reduce to conditionals. In them, the assumption is part of the subject itself: no definite nature has been formed, not at all in the case of impossible things, or in the mind in the case of God. This is different from first taking a fully formed subject and then making a claim about it only under some added condition.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01041
IV. Further clarification and refinement
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01042

Some later thinkers could not answer all the objections to mental existence. They therefore chose another view: what exists in the mind is not the thing known itself, but a shadow or image that resembles it in some way. Here is their reasoning. Proof and experience both show that when we understand something, an image of it appears in the mind. Through it, the mind becomes aware of those things, makes judgments about them, and speaks about them. But because of the objections already raised, they say that the things themselves cannot exist in the mind. The view that seems to satisfy both proof and experience is that what appears in the mind is a shadow or model of the thing known. It resembles the thing the way a spoken word or written mark resembles its meaning. But words and writing resemble meanings by agreement; mental images resemble them by nature.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01043

We object that if the proofs for mental existence work, they show that the very things known exist in the mind—not something separate from them, as writing and spoken sounds are separate. No one says that the written name “Zayd,” or the spoken word for him, is Zayd himself. But our understanding of a thing is different: we make judgments about it and describe what belongs to it, both by nature and by added features. So this proposal does not reconcile proof with experience. It sets both aside and introduces a third view.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01044

A distinguished scholar offered a subtler answer that comes close to the truth. I shall give his argument and the objections to it, so that we can see the issue more clearly. First, he assumes that a thing’s nature follows its existence. That is, unless something exists, it is not any kind of nature at all. Pure nonexistence has no nature and is nothing. Until something has become real in some way, either in the mind or outside it, it is not a nature of any kind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01045

Someone may ask: what is the thing that first exists and then becomes a nature? Is it that very nature? Then the nature exists before it becomes itself, which is plainly impossible. Or is it a different nature? That is even worse: it would be like saying that a horse came to exist and then became a human being.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01046

The answer is that these are not the only choices. First, this is a matter of what comes first in explanation, not what comes first in time. At one level, neither side of a contradiction need apply, as we will explain later. Second, “it exists and becomes human” does not mean that a particular thing first appears and then turns into a human being. The same thing is both human and existent, but it is first real as an existing thing, and only then understood as the nature “human being.” If the objection were sound, we would also have to say that the number four cannot be prior to being even. If four existed first and only later became even, it would either already be even, making “even” prior to itself, or not be even, in which case four would first be odd and later become even. Both conclusions are obviously false.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01047

The scholar now draws his conclusion. In this order of explanation, existence comes first. Only then can we say what kind of thing it is. If we set existence aside, there is no nature left to consider. Mental existence and external existence are truly different. So when something that exists outside the mind comes to exist in the mind, its nature may change too. Outside the mind, a thing has a nature such as substance, quantity, or one of the other basic kinds. When it exists in the mind, its nature changes and becomes a mental quality. This removes the objections, since they all assume that a thing keeps its external nature when it exists in the mind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01048

Someone may object that this is just the copy-and-shadow view: what exists in the mind would not be the thing itself but something that differs from it in nature. The scholar replies that a thing has no fixed nature apart from its modes of existence. An external thing becomes a mental quality when it exists in the mind; a mental quality, if it exists outside the mind, becomes the very thing known. If “the thing itself exists in the mind” means that it exists there even though its nature changes with its mode of existence, then the claim is true. But if it means that the thing keeps exactly the same external nature in the mind, there is no proof for that. The proof only requires that something be present to the mind so it can make a judgment about it. The judgment is about what the thing is in itself, not about how it exists in the mind. So there must be something in the mind that, if it existed outside the mind, would have the feature named by the judgment—even if its nature changes when its mode of existence changes.
